query: For high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what testable methodological hypothesis could enable improved combinations of strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance? Explain why it should work, what measurable improvement is expected relative to the state of the art, the conditions under which it should or should not hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experimental result that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Tailored thermo‐mechanical processing that induces a refined, duplex lamellar (in situ composite) microstructure in Cr‐enhanced eutectic high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) will produce a simultaneous improvement in strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance compared to standard processing routes.
generation.material_initial_state: High‐entropy alloys produced by standard casting or conventional processing with a relatively homogeneous microstructure and lower Cr-content.
generation.intervention: Introduce a combined processing treatment—optimizing casting followed by controlled rolling and annealing—in alloys with an adjusted composition that increases local Cr content to promote micro‐phase separation and create a hierarchical duplex (lamellar) structure.
generation.conditions: The improvement is expected when the alloy composition (especially Cr content) and processing parameters (temperature, deformation, annealing time) are tuned to reliably form the dual-phase lamellar microstructure. The effect may not hold if the composition deviates from the optimal range or if processing conditions fail to induce sufficient phase decomposition.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined duplex lamellar microstructure where nanoscale Cr-rich or stabilization phases are interleaved with a softer matrix, establishing a two-hierarchical constraint that improves both load distribution and crack-arresting capabilities.
generation.mechanism: The dual-phase architecture creates local barriers to deformation and crack propagation. Cr-rich regions (as indicated in PMC10179711) enhance resistance to localized deformation while the lamellar architecture (as shown in PMC6353877) provides in situ composite behavior. This synergy supports improved work hardening, delaying local necking and fracture, and also improves effective stiffness and toughness via stable interfacial bonding (supported by PMC9268215).
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to conventional HEAs or comparable state-of-the-art materials (e.g., AISI 304 or as-cast HEAs), the intervention is predicted to increase yield strength by approximately 10-20%, improve ductility by around 10-15% (measured as percent elongation at failure), and enhance Young’s modulus by 5-10%, along with a corresponding improvement in fracture resistance.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties of standard as‐cast or homogeneously processed high‐entropy alloys, where no tailored microstructure is developed.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable under conditions where controlled processing reliably induces the desired duplex lamellar architecture and when optimized Cr levels are maintained. It may not hold if processing variations or compositional deviations prevent the formation of the targeted microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements depend on the precise alloy system and processing conditions. While preliminary evidence (from PMC10179711, PMC6353877, and PMC9268215) supports a beneficial role for such microstructures, the magnitude of property enhancements is uncertain and will need systematic experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples with identical base compositions. Process one set using the tailored thermo-mechanical protocol (optimized casting, controlled rolling, and annealing to induce a duplex lamellar microstructure with enhanced Cr content) and process the control set using standard processing. Perform a series of mechanical tests including tensile, compression, and fracture toughness evaluations under identical environmental conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements (e.g., at least approximately 10-20% increase in yield strength, 10-15% increase in ductility, and 5-10% increase in Young’s modulus, and enhanced fracture resistance) over the control group, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. The present work reports the interfacial behaviors and mechanical properties of AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) reinforced aluminum matrix composites (AMCs) based on first-principles calculations. It is found the stability of HEA-reinforced AMCs is strongly dependent on the local chemical compositions in the interfacial regions, i.e., those regions containing more Ni atoms (>25%) or fewer Al atoms (<20%) render more stable interfaces in the HEA-reinforced AMCs. It is calculated that the interfacial energy of Al(001)/Al20Co19Cr19Fe19Ni19(001) interfaces varies from −0.242 eV/Å2 to −0.192 eV/Å2, suggesting that the formation of interfaces at (100) atomic plane is energetically favorable. For those constituent alloy elements presented at the interfaces, Ni could stabilize the interface whereas Al tends to deteriorate the stability of interface. It is determined that although the HEA-reinforced AMCs have less yield strength compared to aluminum, their Young’s modulus is enhanced from 69 GPa for pure Al to 134 GPa.
